The UN Fact-Finding Mission found evidence linking UAE-based individuals and entities to arms supplies for the RSF (Sept 2026). The UAE denies arming the RSF.

A draft report by the UN Panel of Experts on Sudan put the number at 1,500 to 2,000 (The Defense Post, July 2026).

claim: An Abu Dhabi company recruited those contractors and moved them through UAE military bases
evidence: HRW cites corporate records, leaked emails and contractor interviews placing recruits at Ghiyathi and Al Wathba (May 2026). Separately, the UN Fact-Finding Mission cited witness testimony that some contractors were flown to the UAE for two months of training at a military-style facility in Ghayathi (Sept 2026). A draft report by the UN Panel of Experts on Sudan, reviewed by Reuters, found the contractors were hired by a UAE-based firm, Global Security Services Group (Reuters, July 2026), and Bloomberg reported on November 6, 2026 that the UN had found the UAE backed the contractors (Bloomberg). The UAE rejects the allegations as a "false media campaign" (allAfrica).

claim: Emirati drones launched from Ethiopia's Bahir Dar airport attacked Khartoum in May 2026
evidence: Sudan's army said drone attacks since March 1, including the May 4 strike on Khartoum airport, were launched from Bahir Dar airport, citing data from a drone shot down in mid-March that it linked to the airport and to the UAE (Reuters, May 5, 2026). Officials gave the serial number of a drone they said was Emirati property (Sudan Tribune), and Sudan recalled its ambassador to Ethiopia. Ethiopia rejected the accusations and accused Sudan's military of backing fighters linked to the TPLF (The East African). The UAE denied that an Emirati drone was used (Reuters, May 6, 2026). No independent verification of the material Sudan presented was found.
